opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core issue is that reinforcement learning agents are fundamentally bottlenecked by the environments we can give them. If you look at what's happened in language and vision, a lot of the progress came from scaling up data: just enormous, diverse corpora pulled from the internet. But in RL, the agent has to interact. It needs an environment that responds to its actions, and historically those environments have been hand-built. Someone has to sit down and write a simulator or design a game, and that's slow, expensive, and ends up being pretty narrow. You get an agent that's really good at Atari, or really good at one robotics task, but it doesn't transfer well, because the world it learned in was so limited.

So the idea of *learning* the environment itself, rather than hand-engineering it, is really appealing. There's this huge amount of video out there of people playing games, of the world just unfolding, and if you can train a model that takes in that video and learns a controllable, interactive world from it, then suddenly you have a way to generate an essentially unlimited variety of environments. You're not limited to what a team of engineers can build; you're limited by the diversity of the data, which is massive.

And I think that matters for generality in a couple of ways. One is just breadth. If you want an agent that can adapt to new situations, it needs to have been trained on a wide distribution of situations, and a learned world model can give you that open-endedness. The other is that it gives you a kind of curriculum lever. If you can generate environments, you can start thinking about generating the *right* environments for where the agent currently is, ones that are challenging but learnable, which is something that's really hard to do when every new environment is a big engineering project.

One of the interesting challenges is that most of that video doesn't come with action labels. You see what happened, but not what button someone pressed. So part of what we've been excited about is learning latent actions directly from the video, essentially discovering what the controllable factors are, so the model becomes playable even though it was never told what the actions were. That's what unlocks using internet-scale video as a source of interactive environments rather than just passive observation.

So, big picture, I see it as a path toward the same kind of scaling story we've seen elsewhere, but for agents: instead of scaling static datasets, you're scaling the worlds that agents get to learn in.

r001.rationale: The response says hand-built environments are slow, expensive, and narrow, and that training is limited by what engineers can build. This communicates that manually adding environments does not scale.

r002.rationale: The response describes learning controllable, playable worlds from video and generating environments for agents to learn in, conveying interactivity through learned environments rather than requiring interaction with the original world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that if you look at what has driven progress in other areas of machine learning, it's scale, and specifically scale of data. Language models got better because we trained them on more and more text. Vision models got better because we trained on more and more images. Reinforcement learning hasn't really had its equivalent of that, and I think a big reason is that RL is bottlenecked on environments, not just on data.

An RL agent doesn't learn from a static dataset. It learns by acting, seeing what happens, and acting again. So to train an agent that generalizes broadly, you need it to have experienced a really broad distribution of worlds, with different dynamics, different goals, different visual appearances, different ways that its actions play out. And today the way we get those worlds is that people hand-build them. Someone writes a simulator, or wires up a game engine, or sets up a physical robot. That's slow and expensive, and it means the set of environments an agent ever sees is basically fixed by how much engineering effort you're willing to put in. If you train on a handful of Atari games or a few MuJoCo tasks, you get an agent that's good at those and often falls over on anything slightly different.

So the question we asked was, what if the environment itself were a learned object rather than a hand-coded one? There is an enormous amount of video out on the internet of people doing things in interactive settings, playing games, operating robots, walking through spaces. That video implicitly contains the dynamics of those worlds. If you can learn a model from it that lets you take an action and see what the next frame looks like, then you suddenly have a source of environments that scales the same way the rest of machine learning scales, with data and compute rather than with engineering hours.

And the interesting part, and the part that was hard, is doing that without having action labels. Most of that video has no record of which button was pressed or which joint was moved. So the model has to discover a latent notion of action on its own, from the structure of how frames change over time. Once it has that, you can prompt it with a frame, maybe a sketch or a photo or a generated image, and then step through it interactively, choosing actions and getting consistent responses back. That is, essentially, an environment that you made from nothing but an image.

Why that matters for generalist agents is that you now have a way to generate essentially unlimited, diverse training worlds. You can train an agent across all of them, and because the diversity is coming from the data distribution rather than from a designer's imagination, it is more likely to reflect the kind of variation the agent will actually encounter. There's also a nice connection to planning. If the agent has a model of how the world responds to its actions, it can imagine the consequences before it commits to them, which is something humans do constantly.

I'd also say I'm interested in this beyond just the agent training story. The idea that anyone can draw a picture and then step into it and play around is a pretty compelling thing on its own. But from the perspective of the field, I think learned environments are the missing piece that could let RL ride the same scaling curve everything else has been on.

r001.rationale: The response says hand-building environments is slow and expensive, and that the environments an agent sees are limited by engineering effort, making it difficult to train for broad generalization.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a model that responds to actions with predicted frames, letting an agent interact with a learned environment instead of requiring it to act in the original world.

astra-6.text:
Well, if we want an agent that can learn to do lots of different things, we need environments that give it lots of different experiences. With reinforcement learning, that’s a real bottleneck, because someone usually has to build those environments and define how the agent can interact with them. And the things we build inevitably cover only a small slice of what we might want an agent to learn.

So the exciting idea is: can we learn models of environments from data, and then let agents interact with those models? Rather than just observing what happened in a video, for example, an agent could take an action and explore what might happen next. That could give us a much broader source of training experiences.

The challenge is making sure those learned environments actually capture the consequences of actions. Looking realistic isn’t enough. They need to support meaningful interaction so that what the agent learns is useful beyond the model itself.

r001.rationale: It says environments usually have to be built and defined by someone, and that these cover only a small slice of what agents may need to learn, identifying manual environment creation as a bottleneck for generalist training.

r002.rationale: It proposes learning environment models from data and letting agents interact with those models by taking actions and exploring outcomes, rather than directly interacting with the underlying environment.

sol-6.1.text:
If we want reinforcement learning agents to be generalists, they need experience across a wide range of environments. An agent can become very good at one game or one task without learning skills that transfer when the world changes. But building lots of interactive environments by hand is expensive, and it limits the variety of experience we can give an agent.

Learning to generate environments offers a way to scale that experience. The important part is that they’re interactive: the agent can take an action, see what happens, and learn from the consequences. That’s different from simply observing examples of someone else acting.

Of course, variety alone isn’t enough. The environments need to have meaningful structure and respond consistently to actions. But if we can learn that kind of environment, we have a potentially much richer source of training experience for agents that need to adapt to new tasks.

r001.rationale: It says building many environments by hand is expensive and limits the variety of training experience, communicating that manual expansion does not scale.

r002.rationale: It describes interactive learned environments, but does not state that they let the agent interact without being placed in the underlying environment itself.
